Measuring network quantum steerability utilizing artificial neural networks
Mengyan Li,1, 2, 3 Yanning Jia,1, 2, 3 Fenzhuo Guo,1, 2, 3, ∗Haifeng Dong,4 Sujuan Qin,3 and Fei Gao3
1School of Science, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing 100876, China

Network quantum steering plays a pivotal role in quantum information science, enabling robust
certification of quantum correlations in scenarios with asymmetric trust assumptions among network parties. Despite its significance, efficient methods for measuring network quantum steerability
remain elusive. To tackle this issue, we develop a neural network-based method that can be generalized to arbitrary quantum networks, providing an effective framework for steerability analysis.
Our method demonstrates remarkable accuracy and efficiency in single-source scenarios, specifically
bipartite and multipartite steering scenarios, with numerical simulations involving isotropic states
and noisy GHZ states showing consistent results with established findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility in the bilocal steering scenario, where an untrusted central party shares two-qubit
isotropic states of different visibilities, ν and ω, with trusted endpoint parties and performs a single
Bell state measurement (BSM). Through explicit construction of network local hidden state (NLHS)
model derived from numerical results and incorporation of the entanglement properties of network
assemblages, we analytically demonstrate that the threshold for the existence of network steering is
determined by the curve νω = 1/3 under the corresponding configuration.
I.
INTRODUCTION
Quantum steering, a fundamental form of quantum
correlation that occupies an intermediate position between quantum entanglement [1] and Bell nonlocality [2],
has emerged as a crucial resource with widespread applications in quantum key distribution, sub-channel discrimination, and quantum teleportation [3, 4]. This seminal concept, initially proposed by Schr¨odinger [5, 6] and
later rigorously formalized by Wiseman et al. [7]. From
a contemporary theoretical perspective, steering refers to
the phenomenon where the subnormalized states of the
trusted party, following measurements performed by the
untrusted party, do not admit a local hidden state (LHS)
model [7]. In light of this, the detection of steering has
garnered significant attention, resulting in the derivation
of various criteria related to steering (refer to Sec. II of
Ref. [4] for a comprehensive review). Notably, the measure of quantum steerability has evolved into a crucial
research direction, giving rise to several operational measures including steering weight [8], steering robustness
[9, 10], and steering cost [11], complemented by various
geometric quantification techniques [12–17] that provide
deeper insights into the nature of quantum steering.
In 2021, Jones et al. [18] pioneered the investigation of
quantum steering in network scenarios, focusing primarily on linear networks consisting of trusted endpoint parties and untrusted intermediate parties. Network steering manifests when the resulting subnormalized states
of the trusted parties, following measurements by all untrusted parties, do not admit a network local hidden state

of network steering gradually deepened into two-forked
tree-shaped networks [19], star networks [20, 21], swapsteering scenario [22] and repeater networks [23], with
these extensions primarily grounded in inequality-based
criteria.
Although the detection of network steering has been
extensively developed, efficient methods for measuring
network quantum steerability remain elusive.
The inherent challenges stem from the intricate nature of network structures, particularly due to the constraints imposed by the independence of sources, which hinder the
applicability of traditional methods.
Fortunately, machine learning techniques, particularly artificial neural
networks (ANNs) [24], present a promising alternative
for tackling these challenges. These intelligent algorithms
offer the potential to transcend the limitations of conventional methods by effectively handling the complex relationships and high-dimensional parameter spaces characteristic of network steering scenarios.
To date, ANNs have been successfully applied to
steering detection in bipartite steering scenario [25–27].
Specifically, Ref. [25] utilized an error backpropagation
neural network to construct high-performance quantum
steering classifiers, enabling precise prediction of steering threshold for generalized Werner states. Developing
this further, Ref. [26] introduced an innovative aggregate class distribution neural network, which not only
improved the accuracy of quantum steering classification
but also refined the steering threshold for generalized
Werner states. Additionally, Ref. [27] leveraged ANNs
to assess the steerability of quantum states with specific
numbers of measurement settings that form a hierarchical
structure, offering new perspectives on the hierarchical

To validate our method, we apply it to well-studied

the network assemblages, we analytically determine the
threshold for the existence of network steering in this
configuration.

Ref. [16] investigated a related problem in the bipartite
steering scenario, but their approach was limited to two-dimensional quantum systems, which constrains its
applicability. In contrast, our method leverages the power
of artificial neural networks (ANNs) to model the causal
relations inherent in quantum networks, thereby enabling
the handling of complex systems with arbitrary dimensions.
To implement this, we employ a two-step approach:
First, we establish a mapping from the input variables
associated with the quantum network to the output variables
through the use of ANNs, which are inherently structured as
directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that mirror the topology of
quantum networks.
Then, we utilize the trained ANNs to approximate the
NLHS model, effectively capturing the causal dependencies
and intricate relationships within the quantum network.
Despite the presence of multiple nonlinearities, the
structure of ANNs provides a flexible framework for accurately modeling the quantum network's causal relations.
Once the ANNs are properly trained, the optimization
problem (6) can be addressed by employing standard
optimization techniques, such as gradient descent, to
minimize the DA metric.

IV.
NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS AND RESULTS

We perform numerical simulations to validate our method in single-source scenarios, including bipartite and multipartite steering scenarios, as well as the bilocal steering scenario. The numerical results demonstrate that our method yields accurate and efficient results, matching established findings in Refs. [16, 28–30].

In the bipartite steering scenario involving isotropic states, our method accurately predicts the steering threshold for generalized Werner states, as demonstrated in Ref. [25]. Similarly, in the multipartite steering scenario involving noisy GHZ states, our method accurately classifies the steering threshold for generalized GHZ states, as shown in Ref. [26]. Furthermore, in the bilocal steering scenario, our method successfully determines the steering threshold for generalized Bell states, as elaborated in Ref. [27].

To validate our method in the bilocal steering scenario, we
construct a specific network architecture where an untrusted central party shares two-qubit isotropic states with trusted endpoint parties and performs a single Bell state measurement (BSM). By explicitly constructing the NLHS model from the numerical results and incorporating the entanglement properties of the network assemblages, we analytically determine the threshold for the existence of network steering in this configuration. The numerical simulation yields results that are consistent with the analytically derived threshold, confirming the accuracy and effectiveness of our method.

V.
ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION

We analyze the numerical results and compare them with established findings. Our method demonstrates remarkable consistency with the known thresholds for steering in the bipartite and multipartite scenarios, as well as in the bilocal scenario. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings, highlighting the potential of ANNs in addressing complex quantum network scenarios.

VI.
CONCLUSION

In this study, we developed a neural network-based method for measuring network quantum steerability. By introducing a well-defined metric and employing ANNs to model causal relationships, we effectively address the challenge of efficiently measuring quantum steerability in complex network scenarios. Numerical simulations validate our method across various single-source scenarios, demonstrating its accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we successfully apply our method to the bilocal steering scenario, confirming the threshold for the existence of network steering. Our results suggest that ANNs offer a promising alternative for tackling the measurement of quantum steerability in network scenarios, especially when faced with the complexities of high-dimensional parameter spaces and intricate network architectures.
